newsitem.title: USA: Democrats, Republicans swap Senate seats.
newsitem.headline: Democrats, Republicans swap Senate seats.

text.p: Democrats made an early gain in the Senate on Tuesday as they fought to break a 2-year-old Republican hold on Congress, but Republicans fought back by picking up a Democratic seat in the South.

Apparently helped by President Bill Clinton's coattails in New Hampshire, former Democratic Representative Dick Swett defeated incumbent Republican Bob Smith, one of the Senate's most conservative members.
But in Alabama, Republican Jeff Sessions beat Democrat Roger Bedford in the race for a seat formerly held by retiring Democrat Howell Heflin.
Democrats won hard fought seats in Massachusetts, New Jersey, Georgia and Illinois that they needed to retain to have any chance of gaining back a Senate majority.

Republicans retained two open seats in Kansas, vacated by presidential candidate Bob Dole and Sen. Nancy Kassebaum. They also held Senate seats in North and South Carolina, Tennessee, Oklahoma and Mississippi.

Stunned by Republicans winning control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in 1994 for the first time in 40 years, Democrats needed to pick up three seats to control the Senate and 19 seats in the House.
House returns were reported more slowly and it was not clear early Tuesday evening whether Democrats would succeed in their quest.

Voters re-elected two of the Senate's most prominent conservatives -- Jesse Helms of North Carolina and 93-year-old Strom Thurmond of South Carolina who aims to celebrate his 100th birthday as a senator in six years.

Thurmond, who will be 94 on Dec. 5, fended off a challenge by Democrat Elliott Close, to head into his eighth six-year term. Helms defeated the black former mayor of Charlotte, Harvey Gantt, in a replay of their contest six years ago.
Their race was the most expensive among the Senate contests, according to the watchdog group Common Cause. Helms spent more than $19 million and Gantt more than $6 million.

In New Jersey Democratic Representative Robert Torricelli defeated conservative Republican Dick Zimmer for the Senate seat vacated by Democrat Bill Bradley. The race had been marked by furious mudslinging ads from both sides.

In Massachusetts Democratic Sen. John Kerry won a third term in a high-profile race with popular Gov. William Weld. In Illinois Representative Richard Durbin defeated Republican Al Salvi, winning the open seat vacated by Democrat Paul Simon.
In Georgia triple amputee Max Cleland, former head of the Veterans Administration, held the Senate seat vacated by fellow Democrat Sam Nunn, defeating Republican Guy Millner.

Other races went as expected. Sen. Phil Gramm of Texas, who unsuccessfully sought the Republican presidential nomination, was re-elected. In Kentucky, Republican Mitch McConnell won as did Democrat Jay Rockefeller in West Virginia.

Thirty-four seats were at stake in the Senate where 13 Republicans and seven Democrats were seeking re-election. Six Republican and eight Democratic seats were open due to retirements and attention was focused on these races where both parties hoped to pick up seats.
Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate and a 235-197 edge in the House where there is one independent who usually votes with the Democrats and two vacant seats.

All 435 seats were at stake in the House -- including those of 73 freshmen Republicans who were swept into office two years ago in the Newt Gingrich-led "revolution" that brought in the first Republican-controlled Congress in 40 years.

Because of their ties to the speaker and last winter's government shutdown more than two dozen of those freshmen were fighting for their political lives, giving Democrats hope of gaining the 19 seats necessary to win back control of the House.

Going into the election, most analysts believed that the Senate would stay in Republican hands, while the party balance in the House was a tossup. Republicans were hoping to win control of the House in two successive congresses for the first time since 1930.
